# NODDI and Magnetization Transfer

{{< include "includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

---

The diffusion methods in the previous part estimate a tensor, or a set of
crossing directions, from the water signal in each voxel. The methods in this
part go further: they fit an explicit *model of the tissue* and report
parameters that are meant to correspond to biological quantities — the fraction
of a voxel occupied by neurites, the dispersion of those neurites, the amount of
myelin. This chapter introduces two such methods. NODDI models the diffusion
signal as arising from separate tissue compartments; magnetization transfer
exploits the exchange of magnetization between water bound to macromolecules and
free water.

## NODDI

NODDI stands for **N**eurite **O**rientation **D**ispersion and **D**ensity
**I**maging (@fig-ch62-noddi-tissue-model). Introduced by Zhang and colleagues
(Zhang et al., 2012, *NeuroImage*), it is a clinically feasible way to estimate
aspects of neurite morphology — the arrangement of dendrites and axons — rather
than reporting a single summary of anisotropy. It is particularly useful near
and within the gray matter, where a simple tensor is a poor description of the
underlying geometry.

![The NODDI tissue model. The measured signal is modeled as a weighted sum of an
intracellular compartment (restricted diffusion inside neurites), an
extracellular compartment (hindered diffusion around them), and an isotropic
CSF compartment.](images/ch62/noddi-tissue-model.png){#fig-ch62-noddi-tissue-model}

The model separates the voxel into three microstructural environments
(@fig-ch62-noddi-compartment-model). The *intracellular* compartment is
represented as a set of sticks — anisotropic cylinders of effectively zero
radius — whose orientations follow a Watson distribution. The *extracellular*
compartment is the space around the neurites, occupied by glia and cell bodies,
where diffusion is hindered but roughly isotropic. The *isotropic* compartment
is CSF, with a larger, free diffusivity. Each compartment contributes an
independent signal to the voxel, and the fitted parameters include the
intracellular volume fraction, the isotropic volume fraction, and an orientation
dispersion index derived from the Watson concentration parameter.

![The NODDI compartment model and its estimated parameters. The normalized
signal is a weighted combination of intracellular, extracellular, and isotropic
terms; the orientation dispersion index (OD) is computed from the Watson
concentration parameter κ.](images/ch62/noddi-compartment-model.png){#fig-ch62-noddi-compartment-model}

Fitting a multi-compartment model of this kind requires more than the single
diffusion weighting used for a tensor fit. NODDI uses a multi-shell acquisition
(@fig-ch62-noddi-acquisition): low b-values (for example, b ≈ 700 s/mm²) are
sensitive to the hindered diffusion in the extra-neurite space, while high
b-values (for example, b ≈ 2000 s/mm²) help characterize the restricted
diffusion inside the neurites. Twenty to thirty directions per nonzero shell are
typically recommended for a robust fit. The model is fit with the NODDI Toolbox
or, faster, with the AMICO implementation.

![NODDI acquisition protocol. Multiple b-value shells with many directions per
shell are required; low and high b-values are sensitive to the extracellular and
intracellular compartments, respectively.](images/ch62/noddi-acquisition.png){#fig-ch62-noddi-acquisition}

The reason to go to this trouble is that NODDI reports something different from
fractional anisotropy (@fig-ch62-noddi-vs-fa). Voxels with the same FA can have
quite different neurite density and orientation dispersion; NODDI disentangles
these two contributions. For anyone looking for a biomarker that is more
specific than FA — say, one that responds to neurite density but not to
fanning — this separation is the appeal.

![Voxels with the same FA (same color) can differ in neurite density and
orientation dispersion. NODDI separates the two microstructural factors that FA
conflates.](images/ch62/noddi-vs-fa.png){#fig-ch62-noddi-vs-fa}

These specificity claims should be read with some caution. Model-based
parameters are only as trustworthy as the model, and later work has tested
whether NODDI's neurite density really measures what its name suggests.
Lampinen and colleagues, for example, compared NODDI's neurite density against
a measure of microscopic anisotropy obtained with a richer acquisition that
varies the *shape* of the diffusion weighting — combining linear tensor encoding
(a gradient in a single direction) with spherical tensor encoding (weighting in
all directions at once), a general scheme sometimes called b-tensor encoding
(@fig-ch62-noddi-critique). The comparison shows that the tidy biological labels
attached to model parameters are provisional; the parameter is an estimate under
assumptions, not a direct measurement of the tissue.

![NODDI has been evaluated against methods that vary the shape of the diffusion
weighting (b-tensor encoding), which test whether the fitted neurite density
behaves as a specific measure of microstructure.](images/ch62/noddi-critique.png){#fig-ch62-noddi-critique}

## Magnetization transfer

Magnetization transfer imaging (MTI) uses a completely different contrast
mechanism. Water in tissue exists in two loosely coupled pools: a *free* pool of
mobile water and a *bound* pool of water associated with macromolecules such as
the proteins and lipids of myelin. A specially designed saturation pulse
deposits radiofrequency energy almost entirely into the bound pool. Some of that
energy is then transferred to the free pool, primarily through dipole–dipole
interactions, partially saturating it. When the free pool is subsequently imaged
with routine pulses and gradients, its signal is reduced — and the size of that
reduction depends on how much bound-pool material is present
(@fig-ch62-mt-mechanism).

![Magnetization transfer. A saturation pulse excites the bound pool; energy
transfers to the free water pool and reduces its signal. The magnetization
transfer ratio, MTR = (S₀ − S_mt)/S₀, quantifies the effect at each
location.](images/ch62/mt-mechanism.png){#fig-ch62-mt-mechanism}

Because this is an imaging measurement, the magnetization transfer ratio can be
compared across locations. Tissues rich in macromolecular content — myelinated
white matter in particular — show a larger MT effect than tissue that is mostly
free water. This gives MT contrast a sensitivity to myelin-related structure
that ordinary T1- or T2-weighting does not have. A classic demonstration is that
the saturation pulse sharpens the boundary of the central sulcus: after the
pulse, the heavily myelinated tissue lining the sulcus stands out (arrows) in a
way it does not in the unsaturated image (@fig-ch62-mt-central-sulcus).

![MT contrast distinguishes the central sulcus. Left: no saturation pulse.
Right: after the saturation pulse, the strongly myelinated banks of the sulcus
are highlighted (arrows).](images/ch62/mt-central-sulcus.png){#fig-ch62-mt-central-sulcus}
